claim: Increased expression of lnc-FANCI-2 is associated with cervical lesion progression from CIN1 to CIN2-3 to cervical cancer.
source: Increased expression of lnc-FANCI-2, a newly discovered long noncoding RNA, is associated with cervical lesion progression from cervical intraepithelial neoplasia stage 1 (CIN1, low grade), CIN2–3 (high grade), to cervical cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' previous work (Liu et al., 2021) and is stated as an established finding in the abstract.

claim: Viral oncoprotein E7 of high-risk human papillomaviruses and host transcription factor YY1 are two major factors promoting lnc-FANCI-2 expression.
source: Viral oncoprotein E7 of high-risk human papillomaviruses (HR-HPVs) and host transcription factor YY1 are two major factors promoting lnc-FANCI-2 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021) and is stated as an established finding.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of lnc-FANCI-2 in HPV16-positive CaSki cells results in altered cell morphology and proliferation.
source: Using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, we knocked out the expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in the HPV16-positive cervical cancer cell line, CaSki cells. The selected knockout (KO) single-cell clones displayed altered cell morphology and proliferation with changes of cellular soluble receptors, but normal HPV16 E6 and E7 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including cell morphology images and proliferation assays.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells maintain normal HPV16 E6 and E7 expression.
source: The selected knockout (KO) single-cell clones displayed altered cell morphology and proliferation with changes of cellular soluble receptors, but normal HPV16 E6 and E7 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibit significantly increased RAS signaling compared to parental cells.
source: Relative to the parental cells, lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibited significantly increased RAS signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, but decreased response to IFN signaling, along with increased p-Akt and p-Erk1/2 (two RAS signaling effectors), IGFBP3, MCAM, VIM, and CCND2 (cyclin D2) and decreased expression of RAC3.
evidence: This claim is supported by RAS GTPase activity assays, RNA-seq data, and western blot analyses presented in Figures 6, 7, and related supplements.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibit significantly increased epithelial-mesenchymal transition compared to parental cells.
source: Relative to the parental cells, lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibited significantly increased RAS signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, but decreased response to IFN signaling
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis showing enrichment of EMT pathway genes in KO cells (Figure 6).

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibit decreased response to IFN signaling compared to parental cells.
source: Relative to the parental cells, lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibited significantly increased RAS signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, but decreased response to IFN signaling
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis showing decreased IFN-gamma and IFN-alpha response pathways in KO cells (Figure 6D, E).

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells show increased expression of p-Akt and p-Erk1/2.
source: Relative to the parental cells, lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibited significantly increased RAS signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, but decreased response to IFN signaling, along with increased p-Akt and p-Erk1/2 (two RAS signaling effectors), IGFBP3, MCAM, VIM, and CCND2 (cyclin D2) and decreased expression of RAC3.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells show increased expression of IGFBP3, MCAM, VIM, and CCND2.
source: Relative to the parental cells, lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibited significantly increased RAS signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, but decreased response to IFN signaling, along with increased p-Akt and p-Erk1/2 (two RAS signaling effectors), IGFBP3, MCAM, VIM, and CCND2 (cyclin D2) and decreased expression of RAC3.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5E, F) and western blot analyses (Figures 5G, 7B).

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells show decreased expression of RAC3.
source: Relative to the parental cells, lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibited significantly increased RAS signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, but decreased response to IFN signaling, along with increased p-Akt and p-Erk1/2 (two RAS signaling effectors), IGFBP3, MCAM, VIM, and CCND2 (cyclin D2) and decreased expression of RAC3.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 in CaSki cells interacts with cellular proteins H13, HNRH1, K1H1, MAP4K4, and RNPS1.
source: lnc-FANCI-2 in CaSki interacts with cellular proteins H13, HNRH1, K1H1, MAP4K4, and RNPS1.
evidence: This claim is supported by IRPCRP-mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9C and Supplementary file 4.

claim: MAP4K4 knockdown leads to enhanced expression of p-Erk1/2 and p-Akt.
source: MAP4K4 knockdown led to enhance the expression of p-Erk1/2 and p-Akt.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: High lnc-FANCI-2 and low MCAM levels in cervical cancer tissues are associated with patients' survival.
source: High lnc-FANCI-2 and low MCAM levels in cervical cancer tissues were found to be associated with patients' survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 8H, I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: A key function of lnc-FANCI-2 is to intrinsically regulate RAS signaling to impact cervical lesion progression and cervical cancer prognosis.
source: A key function of lnc-FANCI-2 intrinsically regulates RAS signaling to impact cervical lesion progression and cervical cancer prognosis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including RAS activity assays, RNA-seq, and clinical correlation data.

claim: Cervical cancer is the second most diagnosed cancer among women worldwide with an estimated 661,000 new cases annually.
source: It is the second most diagnosed cancer among women, with an estimated 661,000 new cases worldwide each year, and the third most frequent cause of cancer-related death, accounting for 348,000 deaths annually (Bray et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological data (Bray et al., 2024).

claim: Cervical cancer is the third most frequent cause of cancer-related death in women, accounting for 348,000 deaths annually.
source: It is the second most diagnosed cancer among women, with an estimated 661,000 new cases worldwide each year, and the third most frequent cause of cancer-related death, accounting for 348,000 deaths annually (Bray et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological data (Bray et al., 2024).

claim: Persistent infections with high-risk HPVs, particularly HPV16 and HPV18, with sustained expression of viral oncoproteins E6 and E7, contribute to squamous epithelial cell tumorigenesis.
source: Persistent infections in the cervical epithelium with the cancer-associated alpha human papillomaviruses (high-risk HPVs [HR-HPVs]), in particular HPV16 and HPV18 with the sustained expression of viral oncoproteins, E6 and E7, contribute to squamous epithelial cell tumorigenesis (Bosch et al., 2002; Munoz et al., 2003; Walboomers et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature (Bosch et al., 2002; Munoz et al., 2003; Walboomers et al., 1999).

claim: Approximately 31.3% of high-grade neoplastic cervical lesions progress to invasive cervical cancer in 30 years.
source: Approximately 31.3% of high-grade neoplastic cervical lesions progress to invasive cervical cancer (ICC) in 30 years (McCredie et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a clinical study (McCredie et al., 2008).

claim: Most cervical lesions resolve spontaneously.
source: while most lesions resolve spontaneously.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical observation in the field of cervical cancer research.

claim: Progression to cervical cancer typically takes 15-20 years after initial HPV infection.
source: The progression to cervical cancer typically takes 15–20 years after initial infection (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/cervical-cancer).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO fact sheet.

claim: Active host defense systems play important roles in preventing malignant transformation of neoplastic cervical lesions.
source: These observations suggest that active host defense systems play important roles in preventing malignant transformation of neoplastic cervical lesions, and additional factors besides E6 and E7 are necessary for cervical cancer development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that most lesions resolve spontaneously and progression takes many years.

claim: Additional factors besides E6 and E7 are necessary for cervical cancer development.
source: These observations suggest that active host defense systems play important roles in preventing malignant transformation of neoplastic cervical lesions, and additional factors besides E6 and E7 are necessary for cervical cancer development.
evidence: This is an inference supported by the long latency period and incomplete penetrance of HPV-induced cancer.

claim: The Fanconi anemia pathway can be activated by HPV-induced DNA damage.
source: Indeed, one tumor suppressor network, the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway (Niraj et al., 2019), can be activated by HPV-induced DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature (Niraj et al., 2019).

claim: FA proteins, including FANCA, FANCD2, and FANCI, are elevated upon HPV infection.
source: FA proteins, including FANCA, FANCD2, and FANCI, are elevated upon HPV infection (Hoskins et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2021; Santegoets et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Hoskins et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2021; Santegoets et al., 2012).

claim: The activated FA pathway restricts HPV replication and guards host genome stability.
source: and the activated FA pathway restricts HPV replication and guards host genome stability (Hoskins et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature (Hoskins et al., 2012).

claim: FANCD2 mutation stimulates HPV16 and HPV31 genome amplification.
source: FANCD2 mutation stimulates HPV16 and HPV31 genome amplification and also promotes cervical and vaginal cancer development in HPV16 E7 transgenic mouse (Park et al., 2010; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies (Park et al., 2010; Park et al., 2014).

claim: FANCD2 mutation promotes cervical and vaginal cancer development in HPV16 E7 transgenic mice.
source: FANCD2 mutation stimulates HPV16 and HPV31 genome amplification and also promotes cervical and vaginal cancer development in HPV16 E7 transgenic mouse (Park et al., 2010; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mouse model studies (Park et al., 2010; Park et al., 2014).

claim: HPV-positive cervical cancer tissues generally exhibit wild-type p53, wild-type K-RAS, and no overexpression of RAS genes.
source: HPV-positive cervical cancer tissues in general exhibit wild-type (WT) p53, WT K-RAS, and no overexpression of RAS genes (Hietanen et al., 2000; Tommasino et al., 2003; Prior et al., 2012; Fernández-Medarde and Santos, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Hietanen et al., 2000; Tommasino et al., 2003; Prior et al., 2012; Fernández-Medarde and Santos, 2011).

claim: Viral oncoprotein E7 plays a major role in immortalization of primary epithelial cells mainly by inactivation of pRb family of proteins.
source: Viral oncoprotein E7 plays a major role in the immortalization of primary epithelial cells mainly by inactivation of pRb family of proteins (Roman and Munger, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature (Roman and Munger, 2013) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: E6 mediates degradation of tumor suppressor p53 and activation of human telomerase reverse transcriptase transcription.
source: whereas E6 mediates degradation of tumor suppressor p53 and activation of human telomerase reverse transcriptase transcription (Vande Pol and Klingelhutz, 2013; Liu et al., 2009; Klingelhutz et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Vande Pol and Klingelhutz, 2013; Liu et al., 2009; Klingelhutz et al., 1996) and represents established knowledge.

claim: High-risk E6 and E7 are necessary but not sufficient to fully transform immortalized cells into malignant cells.
source: However, high-risk E6 and E7 are necessary but not sufficient to transform fully the immortalized cells into malignant cells (Storey et al., 1988; Barbosa and Schlegel, 1989; Hawley-Nelson et al., 1989; Münger et al., 1989; Halbert et al., 1991), and additional oncogenic stress is needed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Storey et al., 1988; Barbosa and Schlegel, 1989; Hawley-Nelson et al., 1989; Münger et al., 1989; Halbert et al., 1991).

claim: HRASG12V, a constitutively activated RAS GTPase mutation, triggers malignant transformation of E6/E7-expressing keratinocytes.
source: For example, the HRASG12V, a constitutively activated RAS GTPase mutation, triggers malignant transformation of E6/E7-expressing keratinocytes (Phelps et al., 1988; DiPaolo et al., 1989; Schreiber et al., 2004; Narisawa-Saito et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Phelps et al., 1988; DiPaolo et al., 1989; Schreiber et al., 2004; Narisawa-Saito et al., 2008).

claim: Normal RAS regulates cell proliferation, cell differentiation, and cell adhesion through cellular signal transduction from growth factor receptors.
source: Normal RAS regulates cell proliferation, cell differentiation, and cell adhesion through cellular signal transduction from growth factor receptors such as insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) and insulin-like growth factor binding proteins (IGFBP1–6) (Conover et al., 2000; Allard and Duan, 2018; Bach, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Conover et al., 2000; Allard and Duan, 2018; Bach, 2018) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Overactive RAS signaling might facilitate transformation of E6/E7-expressing keratinocytes.
source: Thus, overactive RAS signaling might facilitate transformation of E6/E7-expressing keratinocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that activated RAS mutants can transform E6/E7-expressing cells.

claim: HPV16 E6 and E7 can promote development of spontaneous epithelial skin tumors in transgenic mice, but not spontaneous tumors of the reproductive tract.
source: In transgenic mice, HPV16 E6 and E7 can promote the development of spontaneous epithelial skin tumors, but not spontaneous tumors of the reproductive tract (Song et al., 1999; Herber et al., 1996; Song et al., 2000; Riley et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mouse model studies (Song et al., 1999; Herber et al., 1996; Song et al., 2000; Riley et al., 2003).

claim: Prolonged estrogen treatment is required for reproductive tract tumor development in HPV16 E6/E7 transgenic mice.
source: Prolonged estrogen treatment is required (Brake and Lambert, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a mouse model study (Brake and Lambert, 2005).

claim: Estrogen receptor activation stimulates the MAPK/Erk and PI3K/Akt pathways, both of which are mediated by RAS.
source: Estrogen receptor (ER) activation stimulates the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK/Erk) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K/Akt) pathways, both of which are mediated by RAS (Kato et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature (Kato et al., 1995).

claim: The molecular mechanism underlying estrogen-induced cervical cancer in E6 and E7 transgene mice is not fully understood.
source: However, the molecular mechanism underlying estrogen-induced cervical cancer in E6 and E7 transgene mice is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Long noncoding RNAs are RNAs over 200 nucleotides in length lacking a coding capacity for translation into functional proteins.
source: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are RNAs over 200 nucleotides (nt) in length lacking a coding capacity for translation into functional proteins.
evidence: This is a standard definition in the field.

claim: Evidence is still lacking to support the functionality of the majority of lncRNAs.
source: Although several lncRNAs have been proposed to function in diverse biological processes, evidence is still lacking to support the functionality of the majority of lncRNAs (Statello et al., 2021; Liu and Zheng, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles (Statello et al., 2021; Liu and Zheng, 2022).

claim: At least 14 RNA isoforms of lnc-FANCI-2 are expressed by usage of two alternative promoters, alternative RNA splicing, and alternative selection of two polyadenylation sites.
source: At least 14 RNA isoforms of lnc-FANCI-2 are expressed by usage of two alternative promoters, alternative RNA splicing, and alternative selection of two polyadenylation sites from the genomic locus adjacent to the FANCI on Chr15.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 was wrongly annotated by NCBI as MIR9-3HG in the recently updated RefSeq database.
source: Ironically, the lnc-FANCI-2 was wrongly annotated by NCBI as a MIR9-3HG in the recently updated RefSeq database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/refseq/) and two alternative lnc-FANCI-2 promoters identified for expression of lnc-FANCI-2 are ~10 kb downstream of the non-expressible MIR9-3 gene (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021) and reference to the NCBI RefSeq database.

claim: Both lnc-FANCI-2 and FANCI are upregulated simultaneously in neoplastic cervical lesions and cervical cancer by HR-HPV infections.
source: Both lnc-FANCI-2 and FANCI are upregulated simultaneously in neoplastic cervical lesions and cervical cancer by HR-HPV infections.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: E6, and in particular E7, is responsible for the enhanced expression of lnc-FANCI-2.
source: E6, and in particular, E7 is responsible for the enhanced expression of lnc-FANCI-2, the transcription of which is also regulated by YY1 (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 transcription is regulated by YY1.
source: E6, and in particular, E7 is responsible for the enhanced expression of lnc-FANCI-2, the transcription of which is also regulated by YY1 (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: HPV infection increases YY1 levels but decreases the expression of p53-dependent miR-29a which targets the YY1 3' UTR.
source: HPV infection increases YY1 levels but decreases the expression of p53-dependent miR-29a which targets the YY1 3' UTR.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: Viral E7 interacts with YY1 and facilitates YY1 transactivation of lnc-FANCI-2 promoter.
source: Viral E7 interacts with YY1 and facilitates YY1 transactivation of lnc-FANCI-2 promoter (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: In situ hybridization has revealed that lnc-FANCI-2 is preferentially cytoplasmic.
source: In situ hybridization has revealed that lnc-FANCI-2 is preferentially cytoplasmic, but its function in HPV-infected cells has not been characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021) and data in Figure 2.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 in HPV16-infected cells controls RAS signaling by interaction with MAP4K4 and other RNA-binding proteins.
source: In this report, we demonstrate that lnc-FANCI-2 in HPV16-infected cells controls RAS signaling by interaction with MAP4K4 and other RNA-binding proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by IRPCRP-mass spectrometry data (Figure 9) and functional assays.

claim: Ablation of lnc-FANCI-2 in cells promotes RAS signaling and phosphorylation of Akt and Erk.
source: Ablation of lnc-FANCI-2 in the cells promotes RAS signaling and phosphorylation of Akt and Erk.
evidence: This claim is supported by RAS GTPase activity assays and western blot data (Figure 7).

claim: High levels of lnc-FANCI-2 and low levels of MCAM expression in cervical cancer patients correlate with improved survival.
source: High levels of lnc-FANCI-2 and low levels of MCAM expression in cervical cancer patients correlate with improved survival, indicating that lnc-FANCI-2 plays a critical role in regulating RAS signaling to affect cervical cancer progression and patient outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis (Figure 8H, I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).

claim: Both cytoplasmic and nuclear locations of increased lnc-FANCI-2 ISH signals were found within the tumor nest in HPV16-infected cervical squamous cell carcinoma tissues.
source: We found both cytoplasmic and nuclear locations of the increased lnc-FANCI-2 ISH signals within the tumor nest in HPV16-infected cervical squamous cell carcinoma tissues, but not much so in its adjacent normal tissue areas (Figure 1A/B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 1A/B.

claim: Increased lnc-FANCI-2 ISH signals were not much observed in adjacent normal tissue areas of cervical squamous cell carcinoma.
source: We found both cytoplasmic and nuclear locations of the increased lnc-FANCI-2 ISH signals within the tumor nest in HPV16-infected cervical squamous cell carcinoma tissues, but not much so in its adjacent normal tissue areas (Figure 1A/B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 1A/B.

claim: The increased expression of lnc-FANCI-2 became obvious in human foreskin keratinocytes with HPV16 or HPV18 infection when compared to HFK cells without HPV infection.
source: The increased expression of lnc-FANCI-2 became obvious in human foreskin keratinocytes with HPV16 or HPV18 infection when compared to the HFK cells without HPV infection (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: High expression of lnc-FANCI-2 was observed in two HPV16-infected cervical cancer cell lines (SiHa and CaSki).
source: However, we subsequently demonstrated the high expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in two HPV16-infected cervical cancer cell lines (SiHa and CaSki) and two HPV16-infected low-grade cervical lesion-derived cervical keratinocyte subclone lines (W12 20,861 and W12 20,863 cells), but not in two HPV18-infected cervical cancer cell lines (HeLa and C4II cells), nor other HPV-negative cell lines of HCT116 (colorectal cancer cells), BCBL-1 (body cavity B lymphoma cells), HEK293 (Ad5 E1/E2-immortalized human kidney cells), and HaCaT (spontaneously immortalized human epidermal cells) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: High expression of lnc-FANCI-2 was observed in two HPV16-infected low-grade cervical lesion-derived cervical keratinocyte subclone lines (W12 20,861 and W12 20,863 cells).
source: However, we subsequently demonstrated the high expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in two HPV16-infected cervical cancer cell lines (SiHa and CaSki) and two HPV16-infected low-grade cervical lesion-derived cervical keratinocyte subclone lines (W12 20,861 and W12 20,863 cells), but not in two HPV18-infected cervical cancer cell lines (HeLa and C4II cells), nor other HPV-negative cell lines of HCT116 (colorectal cancer cells), BCBL-1 (body cavity B lymphoma cells), HEK293 (Ad5 E1/E2-immortalized human kidney cells), and HaCaT (spontaneously immortalized human epidermal cells) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No expression of lnc-FANCI-2 was detected in two HPV18-infected cervical cancer cell lines (HeLa and C4II cells).
source: However, we subsequently demonstrated the high expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in two HPV16-infected cervical cancer cell lines (SiHa and CaSki) and two HPV16-infected low-grade cervical lesion-derived cervical keratinocyte subclone lines (W12 20,861 and W12 20,863 cells), but not in two HPV18-infected cervical cancer cell lines (HeLa and C4II cells), nor other HPV-negative cell lines of HCT116 (colorectal cancer cells), BCBL-1 (body cavity B lymphoma cells), HEK293 (Ad5 E1/E2-immortalized human kidney cells), and HaCaT (spontaneously immortalized human epidermal cells) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR and northern blot data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: No expression of lnc-FANCI-2 was detected in HPV-negative cell lines HCT116, BCBL-1, HEK293, and HaCaT.
source: However, we subsequently demonstrated the high expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in two HPV16-infected cervical cancer cell lines (SiHa and CaSki) and two HPV16-infected low-grade cervical lesion-derived cervical keratinocyte subclone lines (W12 20,861 and W12 20,863 cells), but not in two HPV18-infected cervical cancer cell lines (HeLa and C4II cells), nor other HPV-negative cell lines of HCT116 (colorectal cancer cells), BCBL-1 (body cavity B lymphoma cells), HEK293 (Ad5 E1/E2-immortalized human kidney cells), and HaCaT (spontaneously immortalized human epidermal cells) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: High expression of lnc-FANCI-2 was observed in HPV-negative cervical cancer cell line C33A cells with mutations of both p53 and RB genes.
source: Interestingly, the high expression of lnc-FANCI-2 was observed in an HPV-negative cervical cancer cell line C33A cells with mutations of both p53 and RB genes (Scheffner et al., 1991; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR and northern blot data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Northern blot confirmed the increased expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in C33A cells but no expression in HeLa cells.
source: Northern blot confirmed the increased expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in C33A cells but no expression in HeLa cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 RNA is mainly cytoplasmic in HPV16-positive CaSki cells.
source: By RT-qPCR analysis of the fractionated total RNA, we demonstrated that lnc-FANCI-2 RNA is mainly cytoplasmic in HPV16-positive CaSki cells, but nuclear in HPV16-positive SiHa and HPV-negative C33A cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell fractionation and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 RNA is mainly nuclear in HPV16-positive SiHa and HPV-negative C33A cells.
source: By RT-qPCR analysis of the fractionated total RNA, we demonstrated that lnc-FANCI-2 RNA is mainly cytoplasmic in HPV16-positive CaSki cells, but nuclear in HPV16-positive SiHa and HPV-negative C33A cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell fractionation and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The differential subcellular distributions of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA from CaSki to SiHa and C33A cells were confirmed by RNAscope RNA-ISH.
source: The differential subcellular distributions of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA from CaSki to SiHa and C33A cells (Figure 2D) were further confirmed by RNAscope RNA-ISH using the lnc-FANCI-2 antisense probe described above.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 RNA is transcribed mainly from a proximal promoter TSS2, but also from an alternative minor, distal promoter TSS1.
source: lnc-FANCI-2 RNA is transcribed mainly from a proximal promoter TSS2, but also from an alternative minor, distal promoter TSS1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021) and is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Two highly conserved YY1 binding motifs upstream of the TSS2 are essential for the TSS2 transcriptional activity.
source: Two highly conserved YY1 binding motifs upstream of the TSS2 are essential for the TSS2 transcriptional activity (Liu et al., 2021; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021) and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: PCR genotyping indicated successful homozygous deletion of the promoter or YY1-binding motifs in selected CaSki cell clones.
source: PCR genotyping indicated successful homozygous deletion of the promoter or YY1-binding motifs, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR screening data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All single-cell clones with deletion of YY1-binding motifs (ΔYY1) showed 70-80% reduction of lnc-FANCI-2 expression compared to control clones.
source: When compared to all control clones transfected and selected from an empty vector containing no gRNA, all single-cell clones with deletion of YY1-binding motifs (ΔYY1) showed 70–80% reduction of lnc-FANCI-2 expression, whereas the single-cell clones with deletion of both TSS1 and TSS2 promoters (ΔPr) showed >90% reduction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Single-cell clones with deletion of both TSS1 and TSS2 promoters (ΔPr) showed >90% reduction of lnc-FANCI-2 expression compared to control clones.
source: When compared to all control clones transfected and selected from an empty vector containing no gRNA, all single-cell clones with deletion of YY1-binding motifs (ΔYY1) showed 70–80% reduction of lnc-FANCI-2 expression, whereas the single-cell clones with deletion of both TSS1 and TSS2 promoters (ΔPr) showed >90% reduction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Northern blot analysis confirmed the decrease in levels of the two major lnc-FANCI-2 isoforms in KO cells.
source: Northern blot analysis confirmed the decrease in levels of the two major lnc-FANCI-2 isoforms (Figure 3D), with an abundant 4 kb lnc-FANCI-2 RNA derived from a distal polyadenylation site pA2 and a less abundant 2 kb of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA derived from a proximal polyadenylation site pA1 (Liu et al., 2021; Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The parental (WT) CaSki cells expressed ~10 copies of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA per cell.
source: The parental (WT) CaSki cells expressed ~10 copies of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA per cell (Liu et al., 2021), whereas the copy number of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in the ΔYY1-D5 cells dropped to ~5 copies and to ~2 copies per cell in the ΔPr-A9 cells (each averaged from 200 cells, Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021) and RNA-ISH quantification shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The copy number of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in the ΔYY1-D5 cells dropped to ~5 copies per cell.
source: The parental (WT) CaSki cells expressed ~10 copies of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA per cell (Liu et al., 2021), whereas the copy number of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in the ΔYY1-D5 cells dropped to ~5 copies and to ~2 copies per cell in the ΔPr-A9 cells (each averaged from 200 cells, Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-ISH quantification shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The copy number of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in the ΔPr-A9 cells dropped to ~2 copies per cell.
source: The parental (WT) CaSki cells expressed ~10 copies of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA per cell (Liu et al., 2021), whereas the copy number of lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in the ΔYY1-D5 cells dropped to ~5 copies and to ~2 copies per cell in the ΔPr-A9 cells (each averaged from 200 cells, Figure 3F).

evidence: This claim is supported by combined RNA-ISH and IF data shown in Figure 8D and quantification in Figure 8E.

claim: Quantitative analyses showed significant reduction of nuclear MCAM protein in the 35 cells with rescued lnc-FANCI-2 expression when compared to the 54 cells expressing no lnc-FANCI-2.
source: Quantitative analyses of the ΔPr-A9 cells with or without transient lnc-FANCI-2 RNA expression showed significant reduction of nuclear MCAM protein in the 35 cells with rescued lnc-FANCI-2 expression when compared to the 54 cells expressing no lnc-FANCI-2 (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: A cleaved MCAM of ~46 kDa was detected mainly in the nuclear fraction by western blot.
source: Using cell fractionation, we detected a cleaved MCAM of ~46 kDa mainly in the nuclear fraction by western blot (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The increased nuclear MCAM expression in ΔPr-A9 cells was proportional to the cytoplasmic and total MCAM levels when compared with the WT CaSki cells.
source: The increased nuclear MCAM expression in ΔPr-A9 cells was proportional to the cytoplasmic and total MCAM levels when compared with the WT CaSki cells (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The nuclear MCAM signal appeared as a proteolytic cleavage product presumably by the increased metalloprotease ADAM9 and ADAM10 proteins and decreased metalloprotease inhibitor TIMP2.
source: The nuclear MCAM signal appeared as a proteolytic cleavage product presumably by the increased metalloprotease ADAM9 and ADAM10 proteins and decreased metalloprotease inhibitor TIMP2 (Figure 4), as observed in other studies (Stalin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in ADAM9, ADAM10, and TIMP2 expression and citation to literature (Stalin et al., 2016).

claim: There was a significant negative correlation in lnc-FANCI-2 and MCAM RNA levels in 304 cervical cancer samples from the TCGA dataset.
source: The significance of an inverse correlation of lnc-FANCI-2 and MCAM in CaSki cells was further investigated by analyzing their expression in 304 cervical cancer samples from the TCGA dataset. There was a significant negative correlation in lnc-FANCI-2 (being wrongly assigned as LINC00925 by NCBI) (Liu et al., 2021) and MCAM RNA levels (Figure 8H).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Cervical cancer patients with a higher level of lnc-FANCI-2 but a lower level of MCAM in the cervical tissue exhibited a better survival prognosis.
source: The opposite effects of lnc-FANCI-2 and MCAM on cervical cancer survival (Figure 8I and Figure 8H and Figure 8—figure supplement 2) show that the cervical cancer patients with a higher level of lnc-FANCI-2 (Liu et al., 2021) but a lower level of MCAM in the cervical tissue (Figure 8H and I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2) exhibited a better survival prognosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 8I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: KD of MCAM expression in the parental WT CaSki cells in the absence of lnc-FANCI-2 led to reduction of Akt and Erk phosphorylation.
source: As shown in Figure 8J, we found, although KD or KO of lnc-FANCI-2 promotes phosphorylation of Akt and Erk (Figure 8J, lane 2), that KD of MCAM expression in the parental WT CaSki cells in the absence of lnc-FANCI-2 (Figure 8J, lane 3) or in ΔPr-A9 cells (Figure 8J, lane 5) led to reduction of Akt and Erk phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8J.

claim: KD of MCAM expression in ΔPr-A9 cells led to reduction of Akt and Erk phosphorylation.
source: As shown in Figure 8J, we found, although KD or KO of lnc-FANCI-2 promotes phosphorylation of Akt and Erk (Figure 8J, lane 2), that KD of MCAM expression in the parental WT CaSki cells in the absence of lnc-FANCI-2 (Figure 8J, lane 3) or in ΔPr-A9 cells (Figure 8J, lane 5) led to reduction of Akt and Erk phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8J.

claim: MCAM is an lnc-FANCI-2 effector but also could be a trigger of signal transduction.
source: These data suggest that MCAM is an lnc-FANCI-2 effector but also could be a trigger of signal transduction as reported (Wang et al., 2020; Joshkon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference from the functional data and supported by citations to literature (Wang et al., 2020; Joshkon et al., 2020).

claim: IGFBP3 protein has been viewed as a RAS signaling regulator.
source: IGFBP3 protein has been viewed as a RAS signaling regulator (Conover et al., 2000; Allard and Duan, 2018; Bach, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Conover et al., 2000; Allard and Duan, 2018; Bach, 2018).

claim: Recent studies show that IGFBP3 has a variety of intracellular ligands involved in many unexpected functions.
source: but recent studies show that IGFBP3 has a variety of intracellular ligands involved in many unexpected functions (Baxter, 2013; Varma Shrivastav et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Baxter, 2013; Varma Shrivastav et al., 2020).

claim: KD of IGFBP3 expression was found to increase phosphorylation of Erk1/2 by ~70% to ~60%.
source: As shown in Figure 8K, KD of IGFBP3 expression was found to increase phosphorylation of Erk1/2 by ~70% (lane 4) to ~60% (lane 6), but not much so for Akt phosphorylation (lanes 4 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8K.

claim: KD of IGFBP3 expression could prevent lnc-FANCI-2 KD-enhanced Akt phosphorylation in the parental WT CaSki cells.
source: Instead, KD of IGFBP3 expression could prevent lnc-FANCI-2 KD-enhanced Akt phosphorylation in the parental WT CaSki cells (Figure 8K, compare lane 2 and lane 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8K.

claim: IGFBP3 has a separate role on phosphorylation of Erk1/2 from Akt in the presence or absence of lnc-FANCI-2.
source: These data suggest a separate role of IGFBP3 on phosphorylation of Erk1/2 from Akt in the presence or absence of lnc-FANCI-2.
evidence: This is an inference from the differential effects of IGFBP3 knockdown on Erk vs Akt phosphorylation.

claim: 32 specific lnc-FANCI-2-binding proteins were identified, including H13, HNRH1, K1H1, MAP4K4, and RNPS1.
source: We identified 32 specific lnc-FANCI-2-binding proteins, including H13, HNRH1, K1H1, MAP4K4, and RNPS1 (Figure 9C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by IRPCRP-mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9C and Supplementary file 4.

claim: MAP4K4 is a serine/threonine protein kinase that stimulates cancer cell proliferation, invasion, and migration.
source: MAP4K4, a serine/threonine protein kinase, stimulates cancer cell proliferation, invasion, and migration and is recently characterized as a novel MAPK/ERK pathway regulator (Gao et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2017; González-Montero et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Gao et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2017; González-Montero et al., 2023).

claim: MAP4K4 is recently characterized as a novel MAPK/ERK pathway regulator.
source: MAP4K4, a serine/threonine protein kinase, stimulates cancer cell proliferation, invasion, and migration and is recently characterized as a novel MAPK/ERK pathway regulator (Gao et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2017; González-Montero et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Gao et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2017; González-Montero et al., 2023).

claim: MAP4K4 negatively regulates RAS signaling by binding to Ras p21 protein activator 1 or RASA1.
source: and negatively regulates RAS signaling by binding to Ras p21 protein activator 1 or RASA1 (Patterson et al., 2023; Roth Flach et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Patterson et al., 2023; Roth Flach et al., 2016).

claim: siRNA KD of MAP4K4 expression in the parental WT CaSki cells led to ~40% or more increase of phosphorylation of both Akt and Erk1/2.
source: We demonstrated that siRNA KD of MAP4K4 expression in the parental WT CaSki cells, as seen for KD of lnc-FANCI-2, led to ~40% or more increase of phosphorylation of both Akt and Erk1/2 and increased expression of MCAM and IGFBP3 (Figure 9D, compare lane 1 to lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: siRNA KD of MAP4K4 expression in the parental WT CaSki cells led to increased expression of MCAM and IGFBP3.
source: We demonstrated that siRNA KD of MAP4K4 expression in the parental WT CaSki cells, as seen for KD of lnc-FANCI-2, led to ~40% or more increase of phosphorylation of both Akt and Erk1/2 and increased expression of MCAM and IGFBP3 (Figure 9D, compare lane 1 to lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: siRNA KD of MAP4K4 expression in the lnc-FANCI-2 KO ΔPr-A9 cells had no effect on expression of IGFBP3, only a minimal effect on MCAM and p-Akt, but strongly on pErk1/2.
source: Interestingly, siRNA KD of MAP4K4 expression in the lnc-FANCI-2 KO ΔPr-A9 cells had no effect on expression of IGFBP3, only a minimal effect on MCAM and p-Akt, but strongly on pErk1/2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Through RNA-protein interactions, the increased lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in cells and their association with MAP4K4 and other cellular proteins could be one arm to control RAS signaling and gene expression of its effectors.
source: The data suggest that, through RNA-protein interactions, the increased lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in cells and their association with MAP4K4 and other cellular proteins could be one arm to control RAS signaling and gene expression of its effectors (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data, shown in Figure 9E.

claim: HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7 are necessary but not sufficient for development of cervical cancer.
source: HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7 are necessary but not sufficient for development of cervical cancer.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in the field, supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Early studies indicated that other oncogenic stress, such as activated RAS mutant, is needed to trigger malignant transformation of E6- and E7-expressing cells.
source: Indeed, early studies indicated that other oncogenic stress, such as activated RAS mutant, is needed to trigger malignant transformation of E6- and E7-expressing cells (Storey et al., 1988; Phelps et al., 1988; Crook et al., 1988; Matlashewski et al., 1987) and tumorigenesis (DiPaolo et al., 1989; Schreiber et al., 2004; Greenhalgh et al., 1994; Riou et al., 1988; Eiben et al., 2002; Golijow et al., 1999; Prokopakis et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple early studies (Storey et al., 1988; Phelps et al., 1988; Crook et al., 1988; Matlashewski et al., 1987; DiPaolo et al., 1989; Schreiber et al., 2004; Greenhalgh et al., 1994; Riou et al., 1988; Eiben et al., 2002; Golijow et al., 1999; Prokopakis et al., 2002).

claim: E7 has been reported to repress phosphorylation of Akt and Akt-mediated signaling.
source: Moreover, E7 has also been reported to repress phosphorylation of Akt and Akt-mediated signaling (Strickland and Vande Pol, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature (Strickland and Vande Pol, 2016).

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 expression is highly dependent on E7 and YY1.
source: In this study, we show that lnc-FANCI-2, whose expression is highly dependent on E7 and YY1 (Liu et al., 2021), intrinsically restricts RAS GTPase activities and phosphorylation of Akt and Erk presumably by interacting with cellular factors in HPV16-positive CaSki cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: Early reports indicated that p-Akt attenuation by E7 could be abolished by introduction of the H73E mutation in the E7 CR3 domain.
source: Interestingly, early reports indicated that p-Akt attenuation by E7 could be abolished by introduction of the H73E mutation in the E7 CR3 domain (Strickland and Vande Pol, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature (Strickland and Vande Pol, 2016).

claim: The reported p-Akt attenuation by E7 might be mediated by the increased expression of lnc-FANCI-2.
source: Thus, it would be presumable that the reported p-Akt attenuation by E7 might be mediated by the increased expression of lnc-FANCI-2.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the connection between E7, YY1, lnc-FANCI-2, and Akt phosphorylation.

claim: Additional oncogenic stress, such as activated RAS mutant, is required to overcome the lnc-FANCI-2 restriction on RAS signaling for malignant transformation and tumorigenesis of E6- and E7-expressing cells.
source: More importantly, these findings also suggest that additional oncogenic stress, such as activated RAS mutant, is required to overcome the lnc-FANCI-2 restriction on RAS signaling for the early observed malignant transformation (Storey et al., 1988; Phelps et al., 1988; Crook et al., 1988; Matlashewski et al., 1987) and tumorigenesis (DiPaolo et al., 1989; Schreiber et al., 2004; Greenhalgh et al., 1994; Riou et al., 1988; Eiben et al., 2002; Golijow et al., 1999; Prokopakis et al., 2002) of E6- and E7-expressing cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and supported by citations to early transformation studies.

claim: Loss of lnc-FANCI-2 in CaSki cells was found to promote RAS signaling but reduction of IFN responses.
source: In CaSki cells, loss of lnc-FANCI-2 in this report was found to promote RAS signaling but reduction of IFN responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the RNA-seq and functional analyses.

claim: High RAS-AKT-ERK signaling induces cell senescence and inhibits tumor cell survival.
source: However, high RAS-AKT-ERK signaling induces cell senescence and inhibits tumor cell survival as shown in this report and in a lung cancer study (Nieto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in this study (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and citation to a lung cancer study (Nieto et al., 2017).

claim: Some lncRNAs function as RAS regulators by their ability to sequester RAS-targeting miRNAs.
source: Some lncRNAs function as RAS regulators (Yang et al., 2019; Saliani et al., 2022) by their ability to sequester RAS-targeting miRNAs, including MALAT1/miR-217, RMRP/miR-206, and KRAS1P/miR-143/let-7 (Saliani et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Yang et al., 2019; Saliani et al., 2022).

claim: lncRNAs may regulate RAS signaling through mechanisms beyond miRNAs.
source: Conceivably, lncRNAs may also regulate RAS signaling through other mechanisms beyond miRNAs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of this study showing protein-mediated regulation.

claim: Loss of lnc-FANCI-2 in HPV16-positive CaSki and SiHa cells promotes RAS signaling and expression of RAS signaling effectors.
source: In this report, loss of lnc-FANCI-2 in HPV16-positive CaSki and SiHa cells promotes RAS signaling and expression of RAS signaling effectors (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings, illustrated in the model in Figure 9E.

claim: MAP4K4 is a negative RAS signaling regulator in the context of the early embryo and lymphatic vascular development by interacting with RASA1.
source: MAP4K4 is a negative RAS signaling regulator in the context of the early embryo (Gao et al., 2017; Patterson et al., 2023) and lymphatic vascular development by interacting with RASA1 (Roth Flach et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Gao et al., 2017; Patterson et al., 2023; Roth Flach et al., 2016).

claim: Silencing of MAP4K4 in parental WT CaSki cells led to a partial increase of both p-Akt and p-Erk1/2.
source: Indeed, silencing of MAP4K4 in parental WT CaSki cells, like KD or KO of lnc-FANCI-2, led to a partial increase of both p-Akt and p-Erk1/2 (Figure 9D) as reported (Patterson et al., 2023; Roth Flach et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9D and citations to literature (Patterson et al., 2023; Roth Flach et al., 2016).

claim: KD of MAP4K4 in ΔPr-A9 cells led to further increased expression of p-Erk1/2 but minimal on p-Akt.
source: Interestingly, KD of MAP4K4 in ΔPr-A9 cells led to further increased expression of p-Erk1/2 but minimal on p-Akt (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a negative correlation of MAP4K4 activity in interaction with lnc-FANCI-2 on Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a negative correlation of MAP4K4 activity in interaction with lnc-FANCI-2 on Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, KD of MAP4K4 in ΔPr-A9 cells led to further increased expression of p-Erk1/2 but minimal on p-Akt (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a negative correlation of MAP4K4 activity in interaction with lnc-FANCI-2 on Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference from the differential effects of MAP4K4 knockdown in WT vs KO cells.

claim: MAP4K4 protein may function in coordination with lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in CaSki cells to restrict one arm of RAS signaling, but not the other.
source: Thus, our data suggest that MAP4K4 protein may function in coordination with lnc-FANCI-2 RNA in CaSki cells to restrict one arm of RAS signaling, but not the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects on Erk vs Akt pathways.

claim: All HR-HPVs are capable of inducing lnc-FANCI-2 expression by experimental infection of keratinocytes.
source: All HR-HPVs are capable of inducing lnc-FANCI-2 expression by experimental infection of keratinocytes (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: HPV+ cervical cancer tissues express high levels of lnc-FANCI-2.
source: HPV+ cervical cancer tissues express high levels of lnc-FANCI-2.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1 and citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: All HPV16+ cervical cancer and pre-cancer cell lines examined produce lnc-FANCI-2.
source: As expected, all HPV16+ cervical cancer and pre-cancer cell lines examined – such as CaSki, SiHa, W12 subclone cells 20861 (HPV16+, integrated) and 20863 (HPV16+, episomal) – produce lnc-FANCI-2.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No expression of lnc-FANCI-2 was found in isogenic HPV18+ HeLa and C4II cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we found no expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in isogenic HPV18+ HeLa and C4II cells, nor in colorectal cancer cell line HCT116, adenovirus 5 DNA-transformed human embryonic kidney cell line HEK293, spontaneously transformed aneuploid immortal keratinocyte cell line HaCaT, and KSHV-infected B cell lymphoma cell line BCBL-1 cells which are all HPV-negative cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR and northern blot data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: HPV-negative cervical cancer cell line C33A cells expressing mutant p53 and mutant pRB produces a high level of lnc-FANCI-2.
source: However, we did find that an HPV-negative cervical cancer cell line, C33A cells expressing mutant p53 and mutant pRB (Scheffner et al., 1991), produces a high level of lnc-FANCI-2 (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR and northern blot data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 promoter activity in response to YY1 binding was found in CaSki and C33A cells, but not in HeLa and HCT116 cells.
source: Using dual luciferase report assays, we did find lnc-FANCI-2 promoter activity in response to YY1 binding in CaSki and C33A cells, but not in HeLa and HCT116 cells, suggesting the presence of a repressive factor(s) in the latter two cell lines (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished luciferase assay data.

claim: KD of E2F1 had no effect on lnc-FANCI-2 promoter activity in CaSki cells.
source: KD of E2F1 had no effect on lnc-FANCI-2 promoter activity in CaSki cells (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: The cellular location of lnc-FANCI-2 varies from cell types, with lnc-FANCI-2 predominantly in the nucleus in SiHa and C33A cells, but in the cytoplasm in CaSki cells.
source: In the lnc-FANCI-2-producing cells, we noticed that the cellular location of lnc-FANCI-2 also varies from cell types, with lnc-FANCI-2 predominantly in the nucleus in SiHa and C33A cells, but in the cytoplasm in CaSki cells, although both cytoplasmic and nuclear lnc-FANCI-2 restrict RAS signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell fractionation and RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Both cytoplasmic and nuclear lnc-FANCI-2 restrict RAS signaling.
source: In the lnc-FANCI-2-producing cells, we noticed that the cellular location of lnc-FANCI-2 also varies from cell types, with lnc-FANCI-2 predominantly in the nucleus in SiHa and C33A cells, but in the cytoplasm in CaSki cells, although both cytoplasmic and nuclear lnc-FANCI-2 restrict RAS signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data showing that knockdown in both CaSki (cytoplasmic) and SiHa (nuclear) increases RAS signaling (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).

claim: A variety of nuclear and cytoplasmic functions of lnc-FANCI-2 remains to be explored.
source: This suggests that a variety of nuclear and cytoplasmic functions of lnc-FANCI-2 remains to be explored.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: IGFBP3 is a major IGF carrier and enhances both IGF- and EGF-RAS signaling to activate PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK pathways.
source: IGFBP3 is a major IGF carrier and enhances both IGF- and EGF-RAS signaling (Allard and Duan, 2018; Martin et al., 2003) to activate phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT and the MAPK/ERK pathways (Józefiak et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Allard and Duan, 2018; Martin et al., 2003; Józefiak et al., 2021).

claim: A suppressive role of IGFBP3 on Erk phosphorylation, but not much on Akt, was found in the presence or absence of lnc-FANCI-2 in HPV16-positive CaSki cells.
source: Surprisingly, we find a suppressive role of IGFBP3 on Erk phosphorylation, but not much on Akt, in the presence or absence of lnc-FANCI-2 in HPV16-positive CaSki cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8K.

claim: ~99% of circulating IGF-1 is bound to IGFBPs, predominantly to IGFBP-3.
source: Although ~99% of circulating IGF-1 is bound to IGFBPs, predominantly to IGFBP-3, the most abundant IGFBP in human serum
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Case-control studies showed significantly lower IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 serum levels in patients with ICC over the control group.
source: case-control studies showed significantly lower IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 serum levels in the patients with ICC over the control group (Jozefiak et al., 2008; Serrano et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to case-control studies (Jozefiak et al., 2008; Serrano et al., 2006).

claim: An increased level of lnc-FANCI-2 expression is associated step-wisely with HR-HPV-positive CIN and ICC tissues.
source: Consistent with lnc-FANCI-2's suppressive effect on IGFBP3 expression in our study, an increased level of lnc-FANCI-2 expression is associated step-wisely with HR-HPV-positive CIN and ICC tissues (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).

claim: KO of lnc-FANCI-2 in CaSki cells affects the expression of a large set of genes involved in RAS signaling, EMT pathway, and IFN responses.
source: It is obvious from our RNA-seq and human soluble receptor array analysis that KO of lnc-FANCI-2 in CaSki cells affects the expression of a large set of genes, including the expression of increased NECTIN2, ADAM9, ADAM10, ITGA5, MCAM, PODXL2, ECM1, but decreased ADAM8, TIM2, and ITGB6, which are responsible for RAS signaling, EMT pathway, and IFN responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the RNA-seq and protein array findings.

claim: The dysregulation of RAS signaling and ADAM protein activity is implicated in various cancers.
source: For example, the dysregulation of RAS signaling and ADAM protein activity is implicated in various cancers.
evidence: This is general knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: ADAM proteins can modulate RAS signaling by cleaving and releasing ligands that activate or inactivate RAS-related pathways.
source: ADAM proteins can modulate RAS signaling by cleaving and releasing ligands that activate or inactivate RAS-related pathways (Schäfer et al., 2004; Ohtsu et al., 2006; Dang et al., 2011; Kleino et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Schäfer et al., 2004; Ohtsu et al., 2006; Dang et al., 2011; Kleino et al., 2015).

claim: Some ADAM proteins are involved in the migration and invasion of cancer cells, and their loss can promote the degradation of KRAS.
source: Some ADAM proteins are involved in the migration and invasion of cancer cells, and their loss can promote the degradation of KRAS (Huang et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature (Huang et al., 2024).

claim: ADAMs are essential for extracellular signaling and regulation of cell adhesion, and their catalytic activity is strongly correlated to SH3 domain binding of SH3 proteins.
source: ADAMs are essential for extracellular signaling and regulation of cell adhesion, and their catalytic activity is strongly correlated to Src-homology 3 (SH3) domain binding of SH3 proteins (Dang et al., 2011; Kleino et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Dang et al., 2011; Kleino et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2010).

claim: One of the major RAS signaling effectors in lnc-FANCI-2 KO or KD cells was found to be MCAM.
source: In addition to the notified activation of PI3K/Akt and Raf/Mek/Erk pathways, one of the major RAS signaling effectors in lnc-FANCI-2 KO or KD cells was found to be MCAM.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the RNA-seq and functional analyses.

claim: MCAM binds various cellular surface receptors or co-receptors to trigger signal transduction, cell proliferation and motility, tumor angiogenesis, and tumor cell metastasis.
source: MCAM binds various cellular surface receptors or co-receptors to trigger signal transduction, cell proliferation and motility, tumor angiogenesis, and tumor cell metastasis (Wang et al., 2020; Joshkon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Wang et al., 2020; Joshkon et al., 2020).

claim: MCAM is an integral, highly glycosylated membrane protein with three common protein isoforms.
source: It is an integral, highly glycosylated membrane protein with three common protein isoforms (Wang et al., 2020; Anfosso et al., 1998; Dye et al., 2009): two membrane-anchored forms with a long (p113) or short (p76) cytoplasmic tail produced by alternative RNA splicing and a proteolytically cleaved soluble form without transmembrane and cytoplasmic regions (Wang et al., 2020; Dye et al., 2009; Bardin et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature (Wang et al., 2020; Anfosso et al., 1998; Dye et al., 2009; Bardin et al., 1998).

claim: The short isoform of MCAM produced by an intramembrane cleavage may be directed toward the nucleus to regulate gene transcription.
source: In addition to its roles in cell signal transduction (Wang et al., 2020; Joshkon et al., 2020; Anfosso et al., 1998; Dye et al., 2009), the short isoform produced by an intramembrane cleavage may be directed toward the nucleus to regulate gene transcription (Stalin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature (Stalin et al., 2016).

claim: CaSki cells express mainly a cytoplasmic form of full-length MCAM (~113 kDa) and a small nuclear form (~46 kDa), but not the short (~76 kDa) isoform.
source: We found that CaSki cells express mainly a cytoplasmic form of full-length MCAM (~113 kDa) and a small nuclear form (~46 kDa), but not the short (~76 kDa) isoform.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibit high MCAM levels, which was most likely a result of the increased RAS signaling.
source: Moreover, lnc-FANCI-2 KO cells exhibit high MCAM levels, which was most likely a result of the increased RAS signaling.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that MCAM is increased in KO cells with increased RAS signaling.

claim: lnc-FANCI-2 and MCAM levels are negatively correlated in cervical cancer patients.
source: Consistently, lnc-FANCI-2 and MCAM levels are negatively correlated in cervical cancer patients, and low levels of MCAM and high levels of lnc-FANCI-2 indicate better prognosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Low levels of MCAM and high levels of lnc-FANCI-2 indicate better prognosis in cervical cancer patients.
source: Consistently, lnc-FANCI-2 and MCAM levels are negatively correlated in cervical cancer patients, and low levels of MCAM and high levels of lnc-FANCI-2 indicate better prognosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 8I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased MCAM might promote cervical tumorigenesis in vivo.
source: This suggests that increased MCAM might promote cervical tumorigenesis in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference from the clinical correlation data.

claim: The HPV16-enhanced expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in cervical cancer cells might function as a negative regulator by binding to various RNA-binding proteins to block RAS signaling and reduce the expression of RAS signaling effectors such as IGFBP3 and MCAM.
source: Given that the cells with Inc-FANCI-2 KO exhibit increased levels of IGFBP3 and MCAM, and the ΔPr-A9 cells with rescued lnc-FANCI-2 RNA expression displayed remarkable reduction of IGFBP3 and MCAM expression, our current model (Figure 9E) highlights how the HPV16-enhanced expression of lnc-FANCI-2 in cervical cancer cells might function as a negative regulator by binding to various RNA-binding proteins to block RAS signaling and reduce the expression of RAS signaling effectors such as IGFBP3 and MCAM.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on all the experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 9E.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that one of lnc-FANCI-2 functions is to maintain epithelial functional integrity by repressing RAS signaling in preventing malignant transformation of neoplastic cervical lesions.
source: In conclusion, this study provides the first evidence that one of lnc-FANCI-2 functions is to maintain epithelial functional integrity by repressing RAS signaling in preventing malignant transformation of neoplastic cervical lesions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Transactivation of lnc-FANCI-2 expression is largely dependent on host transcription factor YY1, of which expression is regulated by HPV oncoproteins and host miR-29a.
source: Since transactivation of lnc-FANCI-2 expression is largely dependent on host transcription factor YY1, of which expression is regulated by HPV oncoproteins and host miR-29a, dissecting their transcription network on lnc-FANCI-2 and its effectors may further provide novel insights involved in host homeostasis against HPV infection-induced carcinogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2021).
